Beállítom Egy olaszok által vezetett EU-s haditengerészeti misszió vasárnap feltartóztatott egy orosz tankert, ami az orosz árnyékflottához tartozik – írja a Reuters . Az olasz védelmi minisztérium közölte, hogy a Toa Payoh nevű, EU-szankciók hatálya alá tartozó tankert a szicíliai Pantelleria szigetétől nyugatra fogták el, miközben Beninből Isztambulba tartott. A hajó kameruni lajtsromjelvénnyel hajózott, de csak a múlt hét óta. A kapitány eleinte nem működött együtt az Eunavfor Med Irini missziójával, így végül helikopterrel szálltak le a fedélzetre. Egy olasz katonai helikopter repül a Toa Payoh olajszállító tartályhajó felett – Fotó: Olasz Védelmi minisztérium A minisztérium közölte, hogy az ellenőrzés, amelyet egy görög hajó és egy lengyel tengeri járőr repülőgép támogatásával végeztek, körülbelül két órán át tartott, és biztonságosan befejeződött. A hajó személyzetét nem tartóztatták le, mert az EU-s missziónak nem volt erre hatásköre. A hatóságok még megvizsgálják, hogy a tanker egyáltalán jogosult volt-e kameruni zászló alatt hajózni. Oroszország részéről még nem érkezett reakció. Ez már a második ilyen művelet két héten belül. Az EU mostanában szigorúbban vizsgálja, hogy mely hajók próbálhatják megkerülni az Oroszországot sújtó olajszankciókat. Egy korábbi elemzés szerint ugyanis az oroszok napi 3,7 millió hordó olajat exportálnak az árnyékflottával, ami a teljes tengeri kivitelük 65 százaléka. Az orosz árnyékflottával, valamint a hajókat érintő szankciókkal és támadásokkal ebben , illetve ebben a cikkben foglalkoztunk korábban. "We have information that Russia is considering unconventional kinetic attacks against critical infrastructure in the Baltics," Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas in Vilnius said, confirming an online report by the news website 15min. "It is likely that Russia could use Ukrainian drones for this purpose." Advertisement Advertisement Kaunas did not provide further details on specific targets or possible time frames. But he later told journalists that Russia could use intercepted Ukrainian drones to obscure the origin of a possible attack on NATO territory and deny responsibility, the report said. "We are talking here about a possible 'false flag' operation in which a fake Ukrainian drone is used. This is probably the most realistic scenario currently being examined," Kaunas later added to journalists. No immediate danger According to other reports, Lithuania's defence minister also said that Russia has not yet made a concrete decision to carry out a specific operation. Nor is there any immediate danger that something could happen in the near future. Advertisement Advertisement Lithuania and other NATO states were monitoring Russia's planning and had warned Moscow about its known intentions, Kaunas said. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda had previously warned of possible sabotage attempts and hybrid attacks on critical infrastructure. The Baltic state has therefore stepped up security measures at key transport and energy facilities. Lithuania borders the Russian Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia's ally Belarus. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the country has felt particularly threatened. Beállítom Miután Magyar Péter miniszterelnök csütörtök reggel Facebook-oldalán erősített rá arra a kormányzati célra, hogy felülvizsgálják a Mohu koncesszióját és a teljes hulladékgazdálkodási rendszert, a délutáni kormányszóvivői sajtótájékoztatón személyesen ismertette, milyen problémák vannak szerintük a hulladék területén. Magyar arról beszélt, özönlenek a kormányhoz is a panaszok a különféle szeméttel kapcsolatos témákban, felhozta a szolnoki szemétkáoszt, a Repont-automaták gyakori működésképtelenségét és általában a palackvisszaváltás körüli társadalmi feszültségeket. A kormányfő szerint „a magyar emberek joggal várják el, hogy ha van egy országos koncesszor, akkor működjön a rendszer”, a „furcsa és véleményes körülmények között” kiadott állami koncesszió „nemcsak koncessziós díjat jelent, hanem kötelezettségekkel is jár”. A tájékoztatás szerint az első körös felülvizsgálaton az derült ki, hogy a szerződésben foglalt kötelezettségeknek a Mohu nem vagy nem megfelelően tesz eleget, nem a céloknak megfelelően működik jelenleg a rendszer. Magyar az uniós újrafelhasználási, begyűjtési célszámokat hozta fel, és azt mondta, Magyarországnak jelenleg évente 90 milliárd forintba kerül az, hogy nem felelünk meg az EU elvárásainak e téren. Az első eredmények szerint nem elég egy-két csavart megjavítani a gépezetben, hanem a teljes rendszer átalakításra szorul, mondta a miniszterelnök, ezt az átalakítást három alapelv szerint készülnek megtenni: legyen jobb minőségű a szolgáltatás, kerüljön kevesebbe az országnak, és több hulladékot lehessen újrahasznosítani lerakás helyett. A koncessziós szerződésről azt mondta, „nem szentírás”, hiába kötötték meg 35 évre, ha nem jó így, akkor kötelességük hozzányúlni. Magyar Péter szerint a vállalt céljaink sorra nem teljesülnek, például 2025-ig vállaltuk, hogy a települési hulladék felét újra fel kell dolgozni, ehhez képest 36 százalékot sem ért el ez az arány. Eközben pedig a lakosságtól és a vállalatoktól folyamatosan érkeznek a panaszok a szolgáltatás minőségére. A miniszterelnök által kivetített dián az szerepelt, egyebek mellett szemléletformálás szükséges, aminek ki kell terjeszteni az elkülönített gyűjtést ösztönző magatartás erősítésére, és ebben gazdasági ösztönzőket is be kell vetni, illetve adatvezérelt módon kell optimalizálni a folyamatokat. Magyar Péter szerint sem ő, sem a magyar adófizetők nem fogadhatják el, hogy évi 90 milliárdot fizessünk azért az uniónak, mert a koncesszor nem teljesít, ezért az első vizsgálat után még részletesebb vizsgálatról döntött a kormány. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA View image in fullscreen Student activists protest against alleged gang rapes. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA Delhi ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.56 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another. As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.” The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers. From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women Read more Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs. Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi. Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary. Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting. This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”. Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said. View image in fullscreen Students’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies. “We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?” Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night. “Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.” Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”. Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces. She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.” ‘If you saw her body, you will never sleep again’: despair as India rape crisis grows Read more The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families. “I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.” Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded. Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.” Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement , in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform. “My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.” Explore more on these topics Delhi India Rape and sexual assault Violence against women and girls Protest South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters View image in fullscreen A Russian jet-powered drone strikes a bridge in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Friday as Moscow steps up attacks on the capital’s infrastructure. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russian attacks on Kyiv bridges cause traffic chaos Key link between two sides of capital hit again as airstrikes force traffic suspensions on three bridges spanning Dnipro River. What we know on day 1,683 Guardian staff and agencies Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia struck a bridge linking two sides of Kyiv for the second successive day , officials said on Friday, part of an intensifying campaign of air attacks ⁠on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital. An ⁠evening drone strike on the ​closed Southern Bridge was the latest in a series of strikes since Thursday that forced the full or partial suspension of traffic across it and two other bridges spanning the Dnipro River. Long traffic jams snaked through the city in the morning and evening. Before ⁠the latest attack on the bridge, Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, held a city security council meeting, describing the situation in Kyiv as “very dramatic”. The strikes on the bridges and other sensitive infrastructure appeared to be linked to an order Vladimir Putin made in September to scrap constraints on Russia’s air campaign, a senior Ukrainian official said. About 500,000 people commuted from the Dnipro’s left bank to the right bank daily, an economic analyst said. Earlier on Friday, one person was killed and two injured in a Russian drone strike that caused a fire on the ‌upper floors of an apartment building, officials said. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest, two people were killed and 32 wounded in a guided bomb strike , the regional governor said. Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion , as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness. For weeks, the main worry in the Ukrainian capital had been the coming winter, Pjotr Sauer reports from Kyiv . But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they were bracing for is already here. The joint US-Ukrainian reconstruction investment fund has sealed its first ⁠critical minerals deal alongside ⁠four other ​new projects, one of its top US officials told Reuters. The fund, established as part of the minerals pact the two countries signed in ⁠April 2025 after a push by Donald Trump, is focused on five sectors, from minerals and defence to energy and infrastructure. The fund’s projects now ​totalled about $70m, said the head of investments at the US International Development Finance Corporation, Conor ⁠Coleman. The long-anticipated first minerals deal would inject roughly $30m into a “joint investment platform” with BGV Group, a firm founded by Hennadii Butkevych, the billionaire co-owner of Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain, ATB. Russia must ⁠provide humanitarian assistance to civilians in ⁠the Russian-occupied Ukrainian ⁠town ​of Oleshky ⁠as the situation there is “appalling” , a European commissioner ⁠said. “Civilians are trapped under siege by Russian forces ‌without access to food, medicine, clean water ​and basic care. This is unacceptable,” said Hadja Lahbib, whose portfolio ​includes humanitarian ‌aid. A former resident quoted by AFP said there was no flour left to make bread and in the early days people ate pigeons but now even those were difficult to find. Latvians vote in a parliamentary election on Saturday that is likely to keep power in the hands of its pro-Ukrainian incumbent prime minister, Andris Kulbergs , although deep political fragmentation may complicate the formation ⁠of a government. Opinion polls put Kulbergs’s centrist ⁠United List ahead, with about 14% of votes, but followed closely by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power.
